Hanul Îndepărtat

Sarah Beth Durst, Oana Duşmănescu (Translator)

4.11
27,561 ratings5,276 reviews
Rate this book
După o revelație devastatoare, o adolescentă decide să-și petreacă vara ajutându-și strămătușa excentrică să-și administreze hanul pitoresc din Vermont și descoperă un secret magic care îi va schimba pentru totdeauna viața.

Planurile Calisei pentru o vară perfectă în Brooklyn sunt transformate în praf și pulbere când află că iubitul ei este un mincinos infidel. Cu inima frântă și disperată să schimbe peisajul, tânăra se hotărăște să urmeze sfatul mamelor sale și să meargă în Vermont pentru a locui câteva luni cu strămătușa ei, care administrează o pensiune primitoare.

Dar când Calisa ajunge la locație, este șocată să găsească un han dărăpănat, în care s-au cazat doar câțiva oaspeți. Situația se înrăutățește după ce își reîntâlnește strămătușa, care îi dă clar de înțeles că nu este binevenită și îi refuză ajutorul, chiar dacă este clar că are nevoie de el.
Deloc dornică să se dea bătută, Calisa începe să renoveze hanul, alături de fiul amabil și atrăgător al grădinarului. Dar, cu cât rămâne mai mult în Vermont, cu atât devine mai evident faptul că există ceva ciudat în legătură cu pensiunea și cu rezidenții ei.

Ceva aproape… supranatural.

Hanul ascunde un secret magic, iar pentru a proteja locul pe care a ajuns să-l iubească, Calisa trebuie să descopere adevărul despre acesta, precum și despre mătușa ei, înainte să fie prea târziu.

About the author

Sarah Beth Durst

53 books10.7k followers
Sarah Beth Durst is the New York Times bestselling author of over twenty-five books for adults, teens, and kids, including cozy fantasy The Spellshop. She's been awarded an American Library Association Alex Award, as well as a Mythopoeic Fantasy Award. Several of her books have been optioned for film/television, including Drink Slay Love, which was made into a TV movie and was a question on Jeopardy! She lives in Stony Brook, New York, with her husband, her children, and her ill-mannered cat. Visit her at sarahbethdurst.com.

Nilufer Ozmekik
3,290 reviews64.9k followers
September 6, 2025
So far, I’ve read every single book this brilliant author has released, and once again, she’s swept me off my feet. I’m sticking with my decision to crown her latest masterpiece with another magical, enchanting five stars. This novel transported me through shimmering portals into magnificent worlds, bursting with incredible creatures and dreamlike universes described in such vivid, lyrical detail that I felt like I was walking through them myself. At the heart of this adventure are two utterly adorable main characters: Calisa, a good-hearted, selfless, curious, and wonderfully adaptable young heroine; and Jack, a sweet, caring, and capable boy whose kindness and knack for fixing anything make him the perfect companion. Together, they stumble upon the strangest bed-and-breakfast inn imaginable, a place brimming with eccentric guests who come seeking healing, seclusion, and the safety of secrets.

The story opens in Brooklyn, where sixteen-year-old Calisa believes her whole future is planned around her boyfriend Ethan—until she catches him cheating and promptly dumps him. Heartbroken but determined to heal, she follows her two moms’ advice and heads to rural Vermont to spend the summer with her great-aunt Zee. Calisa hasn’t seen Zee or her beloved inn since childhood, but instead of warm memories, she finds a dilapidated shell of the place she once adored. Worse, her aunt greets her with hostility, telling her to return to the city, insisting she’s not a good fit for the inn or its secretive guests. Zee lays down strict rules: don’t pry into anyone’s life, don’t ask questions, and absolutely don’t open any closed doors. Yet curiosity—and a certain handsome boy—make following those rules impossible.

Enter Jack, the groundskeeper’s charming son, whose easy smile and hidden worries make him instantly captivating. Jack encourages Calisa to stay, even when Zee’s frosty demeanor suggests otherwise. As Calisa helps with chores—scrubbing dusty floors, rescuing gardens from invading weeds, baking cakes to serve with tea—she begins to uncover the inn’s mysteries. Its guests are unlike anyone she’s ever met: Mulligan, a night-dwelling gentleman who speaks like he’s stepped out of a Shakespearean tragedy (and may or may not be a vampire); Melidor, a green-haired girl with the unnerving ability to communicate with beavers and unleash ear-splitting screams; and Kendra, a commanding yet elegant woman who seems deeply tied to the sea. Each guest’s room, Calisa discovers, is more than it seems—each door opens to another world, a shimmering threshold between reality and dream.

As she digs deeper, Calisa realizes the inn is more magical—and more endangered—than she ever imagined. The thin veil between universes is fraying, her aunt is hiding family secrets about their ancestors, and the inn itself is on the brink of ruin. Determined to restore the inn to its former glory, Calisa throws herself into the project, even as Zee prepares to give up. Jack, of course, stands loyally by her side, and their friendship—perhaps even something more—blooms amid crumbling walls and enchanted doors.

Overall: I adored every page of this story. The tone is sweet yet mysterious, tinged with fairy-tale wonder, and the setting feels like a character in its own right. The cast is marvelously drawn—eccentric, layered, and endlessly fascinating. This is a book that made me smile, ache, and dream all at once. I highly recommend it to fantasy lovers craving a story filled with magic, heart, and discovery. I cannot wait to dive into Sarah Beth Durst’s next creation and see what wonders she shares with us next.

A very huge thanks to NetGalley and Random House Children’s Books / Delacorte Press for providing this enchanting fantasy’s digital reviewer copy in exchange for my honest thoughts.

"Hi, Auntie Zee," Calisa began. "It's great to-"
"You can stay the night," Auntie Zee cut her off. "But then you have to leave."

After having her heart broken by her cheating ex-boyfriend (and the embarassment was further compounded by the fact that nearly everyone knew BUT her), Calisa was really, REALLY, looking forward to going to Auntie Zee's.

Auntie Zee runs a bed and breakfast and with visions of tea times and cottage-y landscaping in her head, Calisa heads over to help her aunt for the summer.

Only one problem.

"I neither need nor want your here."

Despite Auntie Zee's protests, Calisa decides that she cannot return to her home this early with her tail between her legs. So she decides she will make herself useful.

She helps Jack (the gardener, handyman, and general helper) with repairs, then cleans up the inside...and the more Calisa helps out, the more strange things she notices about the place.

There's the battery-operated tea pot that always turns on when she's not looking. Then there's the fireplaces that don't burn wood. Oh and that one time she opened a broom closet only to find a swirling void.

The longer she stays, the more she suspects this isn't an ordinary Inn...in fact, it may actually be magical.

"It's rare, a place like this," Jack said. "That's why it's so special. It's a place where people can come to escape. A real getaway, for whoever needs it."

Oh this one was absolutely lovely and delightfully crafted!

I truly love all of the worlds that this author creates - and this one is no exception. I have always adored stories where the magic is there, though a bit hidden from sight. I had so much fun puzzling out the secrets of the inn along with Calisa!!

One thing that the author excels at is grounding her characters - yes the setting is full of magic and whimsy BUT the characters are still dealing with very real problems.

Auntie Zee doesn't want to give up her inn and yet she cannot run it on her own. Calisa came looking for a place to lick her wounds but instead needs to find a way to revitalize a family business.

It's such a great way to ground or balance out all the fun magic around the place.

Overall - absolutely fabulous!!

⋆.˚ ☾⭒.˚ This reminded me of the magical aspect of Beauty and the Beast, and I am all here for it. At first, I was a little wary when I started this book because I’m not the biggest fan of reading fantasy. I can watch it–some of my favorite movies are fantasy–but reading it, I had a hard time with. Not only that, I’ve been struggling with reading lately because my mental health still isn’t 100% yet, but I am so happy that I was able to finish this book because I loved it.

I was literally so excited when Calisa started to realize that Faraway Inn was a magical place because that’s what I was here for: magic. I wanted to read a book that would be Anne Shirley approved, and I got it. I don’t want to go into too much detail about the mysteries Faraway Inn was harboring, but let’s just say that Steve the lizard is not a lizard and Auntie Zee is more than just an innkeeper. Ugh, it was just so freaking good!




I loved how reasonable Calisa was, and that right there deserves a whole star. I am so tired of main characters being selfish people with no common sense or emotional IQ, so this was a breath of fresh air. She was super understanding yet didn’t take anyone’s BS, she communicated with others to the best of her ability, and tried to look at all aspects of a situation or circumstance, without jumping to conclusions and causing conflict that didn’t need to be there. I was literally over the moon about this while I was reading because I am not in the mood to deal with stupidity right now. I’m not. 😅

And all the other characters were amazing as well. Jack (lol, I had to check if I got his name right because I forgot 😂) was really sweet and super helpful when he chose to be (😏), and I rooted for the little romance between him and Calisa. Auntie Zee took some getting used to, but I understand her sentiments and feelings. Calisa’s moms were super supportive and genuinely cared for their daughter, which was so nice to read. The guests at the inn were also great, and I loved it every time they appeared in a scene. And Steve, the maybe-maybe-not lizard, was the absolute best. ☺

All in all, this was such a fun and enchanting read, and I highly recommend it if you are looking for a sweet, cozy fantasy story that will make you smile and wish you were a magical creature from another world. ✨

January 27, 2026
Sarah Beth Durst really is in her cozy fantasy era and I can only approve of that. This year she even provides cozy goodness for multiple audiences by publishing two books - another Spellshop companion novel and this young adult standalone. As the title suggests this book is all about a magical inn, but the main character Calisa has to be introduced to its otherworldly qualities at first. After a dramatic break-up she travels from Brooklyn to Vermont to stay with her estranged aunt for the summer. Her plan is to busy herself with working around the inn to keep her thoughts as far away from her heartbreak as possible. But upon arrival the inn is less charming than she remembered, not to say shabby, with only a few quests who barely make an appearance and her aunt is also not exactly welcoming. But the groundkeeper's son Jack is nice enough and Calisa is determined to stay and so she just starts cleaning and baking and talking to the guests. She only slowly realizes strange things, like the tea making itself or guests coming out of the broom closet or a huge lizard that's totally not a dragon. I personally think that the introduction to the magic takes a bit too long. It really only starts a third of the way through and while I really enjoyed the inn as a magical place, it is only fully utilized late in the book. That's also why I prefer both The Spellshop and The Enchanted Greenhouse to this new cozy novel by the same author. They both take place in a fantastical world and while the characters still have to learn about magic, they are not oblivious to it like Calisa is. It still was a cute and lighthearted read. Nothing outstanding to me, but a nice palate cleanser with charming characters and cozy magic. I especially liked that the inn was a calm place of recovery for people who just need a break. Sure, the characters stayed kind of shallow under their quirky surface, and I really don't understand why there had to be a romance when Calisa literally just had the worst breakup ever apparently, but I had a very pleasant time with this book anyway. I would totally read more stories about the inn, because there are basically endless possibilities and now that Calisa is familiar with everything, another book would have the potential to be truly great. I will keep my eyes and ears open for some news about that.

Huge thanks to NetGalley and Random House Children's Books | Delacorte Press for providing a digital arc in exchange for an honest review.

4.6 stars!!

This book was such sweet and cozy fantasy about friendship, family, love, second chances, and discovering your purpose in life. The Faraway Inn follows 16 year old Calisa comes to Vermont to help her great Aunt at her Bed and Breakfast, but discovers that the B&B is run down. Auntie Zee won't accept help from Calisa, but Calisa is determined to fix the inn and has the groundskeeper son, Jack assist her. Calisa realizes that there is something magical about the inn and stops at nothing to find out what it is.

Thoughts
I was completely swept away by this cozy fantasy from the very first page. I appreciated that this book focused on family and building a home instead of battles. I loved the inclusion of fantasy creatures including dragons, firebirds, witches, fae, plant people, a sea witch and more. This book felt like reading a book by a warm fire. This book was so wholesome, I couldn't stop smiling. The writing was witty and descriptive. The descriptions of the food made me hungry. The plot was intriguing and kept me engaged. I loved the splash of magic throughout the book which was the perfect amount for this cozy fantasy. The ending was so heartwarming and beautiful. I'm so happy the conflict was resolved and it ended on a happy note.

Characters
I loved Calisa, she was hardworking, brave, resilient, helpful, caring and determined. I'm glad that Calisa spoke her mind when she didn't agree with something. I was inspired by her bravery and determination, she didn't give up on the inn or her friends. Calisa's character development was excellent, she found purpose in life and opened herself up to other people she cared about. I adored Jack, he was charming, sweet, helpful, hardworking and brave. I loved that over time he opened up to Calisa about himself and was honest with her. Jack was such a cinnamon roll with a heart of gold. The side characters were also great especially Steve (mini dragon), Mulligan, Melidor and Calisa's moms. I didn't like Aunt Zee at first but other time she grew on me and showed a kinder side of herself. I loved the interactions between Calisa and Steve and Mulligan.

Romance
The romance between Calisa and Jack was perfection. I loved that the romance was slow-burn, it took a while for their feelings to develop. The romance was also realistic and relatable. I could feel the deep connection between the characters. I loved that Calisa and Jack listened to each other and understood each other. They let each others personality shine without trying to change one another. The romantic scenes made me giggle and smile. Calisa and Jack deserve each other.

I recommend this book to anyone who loves cozy fantasy, awesome characters and a sweet romance.

For everyone who needs an escape,
a refuge,
a moment to breathe
😌 💖 ✨

This was exactly the heartwarming fantasy novel I needed 🥰 Sarah Durst does cosy fantasy like no other, combining mystery and romance with her gentle whimsical style of writing.

The Faraway Inn sees sixteen-year-old Calisa arriving in Vermont to help her cantankerous Great-aunt at her bed-and-breakfast for the summer. She soon finds it shockingly run down and her eccentric Auntie Zee refuses to take any help. Calisa is determined to fix up the inn and convince her aunt to keep her around for the summer, but the longer she stays, the more curious she becomes…there is something unusual about this B&B…something mysteriously mystical ✨ There is a secret and Calisa won’t stop until she finds out what is behind the closed doors…

I was utterly charmed by this uber cosy fantasy. Sarah captured by attention from page one with her smooth, flowing narrative that was clear and easy to follow. Fantasy novels can often employ heavy world-building but Sarah keeps us rooted in the modern world, allowing her to explore other themes whilst still giving the book a mystical charm. I particularly enjoyed the mystery element to the plot; prior to reading, I hadn’t expected there to be such an in-depth puzzle to be solved. It held my full attention and made it almost impossible to put down. Furthermore, I loved the wholesome family focus. It brought a real sense of grounding to the story.

As for the fantasy side of things, I absolutely loved how Sarah blended the mystical with real world. I hadn’t expected there a permanent smile on my face whilst reading of the array of imaginative creatures including flying lizards, plant people, dragons, firebirds, a sea witch, and more! They were all such unique characters that held strong personalities. The vivid descriptions along side the witty vocabulary was perfect.

Sarah Durst has a great skill at writing memorable characters and that was clearly demonstrated throughout this novel. Our MFC, Calisa, is a hardworking, courageous, caring, and determined young woman. Her motivation and determination to help safe the inn was very admirable and she would stop at nothing. I also appreciated her characters development over the course of the story. In the beginning, she was looking to move on from her ex, but she grew into a new, confident person who had found a purpose and cared deeply for the people (and creatures) around her.

Meanwhile, Jack is a total golden retriever of a boy. I loved his sweet, caring soul and the vulnerability he showed was so genuine and heartfelt. But I also admired him for his incredible work ethic and bravery. There isn’t a bad bone in this guy’s body.

There were also some very strong side characters/creatures including Calisa’s mums, Mulligan, Melidor, Steve, and of course, Auntie Zee. Zee was a tough cookie to crack but she definitely grew on me overtime as her kinder, less guarded side came out. The interactions and sense of found family between them ALL was so heartfelt and uplifting 😌💖

Aside from the major plot, there was definitely romance in the air between Calisa and Jack. This book is actually targeted at YA which was a pleasant change. Their romance was so sweet and youthful. And although Calisa most definitely had feelings for him from the start, it was definitely a slow-burning romance. Personally, I felt this was more genuine and realistic given both their age and the circumstances. It was an understated but meaningful relationship in which they allowed each other to shine.

Overall, this book was a magical feast for the senses. It was everything I wanted and more - cosy, gentle, and mysterious story, unique and memorable characters, and a sweet, loving romance 💕

💖 Finally, I would like to conclude by sharing something special that the author, Sarah Durst, shared with us: ‘Everyone should have a great-aunt with a magical inn. Also, a pet dragon. And enchanted tea. That's why I wrote this book: I believe that everyone deserves a magical escape…Escape is a beautiful and essential tool that enables us to cope with the world more effectively. It's a deep breath before the plunge. It isn't a display of weakness; it's a gathering of strength. It's taking a moment to remind yourself that there's good in the world-that there's wonder and magic and friendship and love and kindness and cake. Please know that there is good out there—and also cake. Please know that there is light after the darkness, and there will always be another door to open.’ 💖

4.5 🌟🌟🌟🌟✨

March 31, 2026
4.25 ★— I think every person that gets cheated on should get to spend a summer in a magical inn surrounded by mythical creatures, while making cakes.

So... this was cute, which is absolutely no surprise to me! Durst managed to enchant me with the coziness of this book just as much as she has with her Spellshop series, only this time through a YA story featuring a teenage heroine, Calisa, who’s lived her life growing up in a non-magical world.

Looking to heal her broken heart, she goes to Vermont to her aunt’s inn that… surprise, surprise, isn’t just a normal inn as is slowly revealed.

This story features a lot of Durst’s staples: interesting and quirky plants, magical animals, otherworldly beings and a very kind male love interest that helps the heroine in her efforts at the inn.

A major part of the story is the aforementioned ex-boyfriend’s infidelity that Calisa is reeling from in the beginning, which I found was thoughtfully explored as Calisa processes the feelings of her breakup and works through those emotions that come with it. I came away really liking the portrayal of teenage heartbreak and the confusion that is common at her age!

The book's other major character, Auntie Zee, was delightfully grumpy! I liked that she actually was someone that didn’t immediately warm to Calisa and that it truly felt like Calisa had to earn her aunt’s trust and respect, and the book did a good job weaving that in with a lot of the familial issues that are present in the story.

Overall, The Faraway Inn was filled with the cozy goodness you'd expect, while still having aspects of a fun mystery, a lot of really cool and different fantastical moments and some well-explored emotional healing that made this all a great read!

A stunning cozy fantasy!
Full of magic, magical beings and lively depicted strange, beautiful, wondrous, faraway worlds in infinite dimensions!

Calisa, sixteen years-old, is spending 2 summer months in Vermont with her great-aunt Zee at The Faraway Inn, after her boyfriend Ethan broke and stomped on her heart!
The last time she was there, with her moms, she was 5 years-old, and remembered it to be a lovely, beautiful and cute place, surrounded by pine trees and flower gardens.
Ater a long and tired journey she reaches The Faraway Inn and can't believe her eyes!
The 3 stories inn is run-down.
Tilted and lopsided roof, shutters hung crooked on the windows and some boarded up with plywood, the porch buried beneath the grown greenery, the garden a mess jungle.

She walks in and falls through the porch.
Jack a boy about her age, handsome, strong and ou-of-a-movie, who is the groundskeeper's son, has to do a task first before he can help her!
So she helps herself and enters the house.
The lobby, the reception desk, the sitting room, the dinning room, are full of dust, cobwebs, half the furniture covered, and it seems like they hadn't been used in years.
She only sees an elderly white cat, Portia, on a chair.
She finds the kitchen, cleaned, but seemed not to be used too.
Where is everybody?
And then her Auntie Zee appears.
She's grumpy, very wrinkled, looking much older than her 82 years-old, and says she can't stay, doesn't need her help.
Just sleep the night and leave.
But after Calisa tells her the reason she's there, Ethan, she lets her stay for 3 days, but must follow her rules: don't open doors without permission and don't ask questions.

She'll stay in room 2, that had once been adorable, smells like lavender, cleaner than the others, but rug and quilt frayed.
Jack and his father live in room 6.
Of course she cant sleep, it's so quiet.
Heard a noise, thought it was Jack and went to the kitchen where she meets the first of the 3 guests, one still arriving, Mulligan, room 8, a very thin man dressed all in black, humming a song, happy to see her, and helps him doing tbe best hot chocolate she ever tasted, "like the warmth of a hug from a friend who just wanted you to feel better."

She told Jack she knew how to do pancakes he loves so much, and the next morning he's already there when she arrives, and the guests will have them for breakfast too.

Calisa wasn't convinced there was anything ordinary about the inn!
The broom closet that first howled, before Auntie Zee closed it and opened it again, the statue of a woman that keeps moving from place to place, the whispers she heard under the porch, Kendra, room 3, that she could swear arrived from the cleaning supplies closet near the refrigerator!

She wants to change Auntie Zee's mind so decides to do some cleaning.
The sitting room, where the white cat usually is, where the teapot starts by itself and the fireplace too, the upstairs bathroom where suddenly, as she opens the towel closet, a huge lizard tumbles out, later named Steve, that's actually a small winged dragon, that is always near Calisa, protecting her, or on her shoulder and that she takes to the greenhouse, later approved by Auntie Zee.
And after that there's no more talk about her leaving the inn.
Next the dinning room, and the garden, with Jack 's help, where she's almost attacked by Melidor, the last guest, Steve to the rescue, a girl with green hair and that talks to plants and beavers.

Jack is always deflecting her questions, and that she could go back to Brooklyn.
Calisa sees he's scared, deciding to find for herself.
She enters room 12, that she knows is empty, opens the closet, no clothes hanging, but with a swirl of colors, walks through it and meets a woman with green skin running after walking flowers, that gives her a message to her daughter Melidor!
Returing to the room she wonders where she went.
Opens another one and finds another swirling portal.
When Jack comes to the kitchen where she's doing a cake for tea, he ends up telling everything he knows after Calisa promises she wouldn't tell Auntie Zee, because she would fire him, and the iin is his home!

The B&B is a nexus of realms, meaning lots of doors to other worlds.
That's why it's special.
A place where people can come to escape, a getaway, for whoever needs it.
Not other planets but other dimensions!
His dad went through one to look for something to help the inn and has been gone for 3 years, because the portal doesn't work anymore and wouldn't reopen.
So he has to come to Jack, Auntie Zee told him.
If the inn doesn't stay in business his dad won't have a place to return to!

And then Auntie Zee goes out to buy supplies for her cakes and doesn't come back!

What will they do now?
How will they be able to run the B&B alone and search for Auntie Zee in the suppliers portals at the same time?
Will the "friendship", with lots of kisses , develops into something more between Calisa and Jack?

The ending is not only amazing but absolutely surprising!!

My first book from this author and it won't be my last!!

I really wanted to love The Faraway Inn, and in a lot of ways I did. Sarah Beth Durst writes cozy fantasy in a way that always makes her books feel like cozy video games to me, very Stardew Valley vibes, and this one fits right in. The inn itself was hands down my favorite part of the book. I loved all the scenes of Calisa cleaning, fixing things up, and slowly bringing the inn back to life. Those moments were genuinely comforting, and the inn felt like its own character.

The magical guests and creatures were fun and creative, and I liked a lot of the side characters we meet along the way. I also noticed what felt like little nods to some of her other cozy books, which was a nice touch. The romance with the groundskeeper’s son was sweet and low key, and it worked well with the overall healing, summer in Vermont vibe.

That said, the book moved pretty slowly for me, and I had a hard time figuring out what the main plot was supposed to be. I kept waiting for things to really kick into gear. I enjoyed the cozy atmosphere, but at times it felt more like a collection of nice moments than a story that was actually going somewhere.

I also did not love the sociopolitical commentary that was woven into the story. When I pick up cozy fantasy, I am looking for an escape, and those moments pulled me out of the book rather than adding anything meaningful for me.

Overall, The Faraway Inn was a cozy, comforting read with a great setting and some really charming ideas, but the slow pacing and unfocused plot kept it from being a favorite. I think fans of cozy fantasy and Sarah Beth Durst will still enjoy it, especially if you love magical inns and quiet, restorative stories. Just do not go into it expecting a fast paced or plot heavy read.

Another adorable cozy read from Sarah Beth Durst! I swear, when almost anyone else writes cozy I’m like “that’s boring,” but SBD’s are always so lovely. I really enjoyed the setting of the inn and it DID remind me a lot of the inn from Clean Sweep by Illona Andrews, so I was a happy camper!

I do think this could have been slightly more romantic… just maybe a few more cute interactions between the two MC’s, and I think I would have liked a few more interactions between her and her aunt as well. I’m not sure what I would really be looking for with those, maybe just a few instances where her aunt let her walls down just a bit so we could have gotten to know her a little better. I get that she had given up on a lot of things at that point in the story, but surely someone with access to magic would maintain some glimmer of hope. I thought her character was just a little bit too severe.

Overall, this was a very sweet read! I also did really enjoy that this was YA just for a little change of pace from what I normally read from this author. I’m excited to read Sea of Charms soon! I just realized it comes out next month, woohoo!

The most lovesick of Durst’s heroines.

Calisa, a teen trying to escape her cheating ex, spends her summer in Vermont helping her reluctant great-aunt run a rundown inn. There are a few peculiarities as well as a kind guy who actually listens to her.

This was sweet and cozy like all of the author’s recent books, but it missed that magical element for me despite it being a, you know, magical B&B.

Calisa can never stop thinking about Jack, despite this entire endeavour supposed to be an opportunity for self-development and to STOP thinking about guys.

I appreciated that the romance was built on mutual respect and helping with each other’s weak spots, but it was soulmates and pining from day one in Calisa’s head.

I wish we got to spend more time with the guests and learning their quirks/growth. Similarly, getting better understanding of the other worlds was not the point of the story, but if you set up a portal fantasy, I am always going to be curious about more.

I would say this on the younger side of YA, despite Calisa being 17 years old.

2 stars. I wanted to like this book a lot more than I did.

My local library special ordered it for me simply because I asked how/when/if they get new releases and this book just came out at the end of March 2026. I’ve never read anything by Sarah Beth Durst (SBD) before but I’ve seen her books on Goodreads and she’s literally been dubbed ‘The Queen of Cozy Fantasy,’ which sounded like something I might enjoy (admittedly, I’ve never read anything before in the ‘cozy fantasy’ subgenre). Unfortunately, though, ‘The Faraway Inn’ didn’t quite do it for me. I was between 2 and 3 stars for this book, but if I’m being honest, the extra star would have been just for the cover and printed edges aka ‘it was pretty.’
But, 2 stars it actually is because of the content inside and that’s what matters after all. Fling open the closet door and step inside this breakdown and review (spoilers ahead!):

PLOT: Just OK 🥞🥞

FMC Calisa needs to get away from her city life in Brooklyn after her high school sweetheart cheats on her with some floozy. She decides to visit her great-aunt in Vermont who runs a Bed and Breakfast called, The Faraway Inn. But when she arrives, not all is as it seems. To make matters worse, her aunt doesn’t even want her there.
Simple set up but the novel failed to deliver. Calisa starts noticing oddities around the inn, like a tea kettle that seems to brew all on its own, a statue that seems to move from one spot to another, and a closet door with a gaping void of darkness and howls. These small magical phenomena are sprinkled in with descriptions of Calisa making pancakes, weeding the garden, baking cakes, and flirting with the groundkeeper’s son, Jack.
Normally, I don’t mind reading about characters doing mundane tasks but this was literally SBD rattling off pancake ingredients and full-on paragraphs of ‘Calisa vacuumed. Then she dusted. She wiped down the mirror next.’ It was boring. And it was the first half of the book. Even when we got to the ‘exciting’ part of the novel, the realization that the inn is sprinkled with magical portals that teleport one to magical worlds, I was still bored.

PACING: Just OK 🥞🥞

Springing off the notion that I was bored while reading this story, the pacing was incredibly slow. For a 372-page novel, this could have had way more content that would have made it a page turner/can’t put it down/have to pick it back up sort of book. I get that cozy reads are ‘low-stakes and comforting’ but it still needs to be compelling, no? Otherwise, why am I reading it? Side note: It bothered me that most chapters never ended on a cliff hanger or a reveal that enticed me to want to zoom into the next one. Every chapter felt like “a good stopping point.” Yikes.

SETTING: Good 🥞🥞🥞

Okay, I’ll give some props to the inn itself for being an interesting setting for our FMC to explore. As I mentioned before there’s a self-brewing tea kettle, closet doors with portals to other realms, but also a dragon named Steve and a sassy magic mirror that got some of the only chuckles out of me during my read. The inn itself is described as being rundown and in need of TLC which becomes the undertaking of our FMC. At first it’s because she thinks cleaning up will convince her aunt to let her stay, then it becomes a matter of ‘saving the inn.’
As for the other ‘realms’ our leads explore? Meh. They didn’t really fascinate me like they did the FMC. She went to a gloomy meadow with a purple sun, the Night Market (a farmer’s market under a night sky - quite a literal namesake), and a seaside town with sea dragons, sea turtles and scaled fish people. Since our characters didn’t stay in any of these realms for prolonged periods of time, nor explore any of them in detail, I didn’t care much when we visited them. In fact, I sort of missed the inn and what else could have been there.

CHARACTERS: Just OK 🥞🥞

I always feel that any book can be saved if it has strongly written, developed and believable characters the reader can get behind or sympathize with etc. In my opinion, we didn’t quite get that here.
CALISA: FMC Calisa doesn’t really have any outstanding qualities other than she’s nosy, curious and insistent on breaking all two of her great-aunt’s rules. (No questions, no opening doors). I did admire that as soon as she arrived, she was willing to roll up her sleeves and get to work fixing up the inn. What I didn’t care for though was she immediately latches herself onto Jack, the hot son of the groundskeeper, even though the point of her coming to the inn was to forget about boys for a while.
Her curiosity is natural. Her internal thoughts rather immature. She has no obvious flaws or internal conflict other than trying to get over a boy. Honestly, the focus on her relationship with ex Ethan and now prospect Jack cheapened her. I would have rather seen her focus on repairing her relationship with her aunt, or her aunt’s relationship with her mom, than obsessing over a new boy.
Lastly, Calisa learns or rather realizes that she has the same magical talents as her great-aunt and can open portals. Meaning, she could eventually run the inn. Taking into account she’s only a 16-year-old girl, I didn’t love this. Had she been a twenty-something adult with an unfulfilling job and in need of a career change, this would have been a welcome thought. But she’s not even out of high school yet and her destiny as the next innkeeper is decided. I don’t know, I just wasn’t into it. I guess we’re trying to end on a happy note, but we would have gotten that simply with her having forged a relationship with her great-aunt and getting to return to the inn anytime she likes.

JACK: MMC Jack works at the inn with his father. Except, when Calisa arrives, his dad is nowhere to be seen. Well, that’s because he disappeared three years ago after entering a portal that shut permanently two days later. Jack is a little lost without his dad, and trying to upkeep the place all on his own, is partially why it’s in such bad shape when FMC gets there. Jack has a quirky personality, says odd things and has awkward timing. Like talking about cheese as FMC is stuck in the porch floor. I think he was meant to be the ‘golden retriever boyfriend’ but he was rather dopey and this didn’t appeal to me.
His clueless and borderline idiotic personality became endearing to the FMC but his best attribute was actually being nothing like Calisa’s ex. Which isn’t saying much. Every time she admired a trait of his (‘Wow, he listened to me. He remembered what I said. He respects me’) This is always then followed up with “Unlike Ethan.” This type of thinking by our FMC just had me going, “Rebound!”
Jack’s real purpose in the story is to reveal tidbits of information to the FMC throughout and be her next love interest. He was safe, he was bland, he was boring. I didn’t feel any chemistry between them, mostly because the dialogue was cringe at times, and I didn’t appreciate such a focus on a love interest in the first place since I thought the story would emphasize Calisa working on herself/her familial relationships.

AUNTIE ZEE: The innkeeper and resident witch keeping it all going. She’s getting older and her magic is starting to wane, thus leading to portals randomly closing with no hope of reopening. Zee is ornery, a woman of few words but plenty of grunts, and doesn’t want help running *her* inn. At first, she only says Calisa can stay for three days but as the girl works hard, bakes cakes, and reinstates afternoon teatime, Zee stops mentioning the prospect of her going home. Then halfway through the story, Zee disappears and our FMC and MMC start entering portals to track her down. Afterall, the inn needs her.
Frankly, I felt we didn’t get enough Auntie Zee. I would have liked more scenes with her and Calisa forging a bond and a relationship (instead of it always being about Jack). Considering Zee admits she knew early on in Calisa’s stay that she had witch powers (activating the tea kettle) it surprises me that Zee didn’t try to get to know her grandniece better or at least tell the truth about the inn. (What a story that would have been; her great-aunt teaching her magic, instead of baking cakes and dusting bookshelves).
Zee loves the inn, yet at the same time hates accepting help, so she’s willing to let everything fall into disrepair? That seemed like a clashing of two ideas but I guess this type of behavior does happen so it’s not totally unrealistic. I did like Jack’s father reminding her she isn’t doing it all alone. He’s been working there for years with his son. Zee needed to be put in her place a little bit and I was glad to see it happen.

WRITING: Just OK 🥞🥞

So, this is also where the story fell flat. SBD’s writing was on the disappointing side. Descriptions of characters, settings and action were lackluster. Even now, I don’t remember what Calisa looks like. I know Jack is ‘hot boi,’ as it was mentioned several times. The inn itself lacked descriptions that made it feel magical, or gave those cottagecore vibes we all wanted. The description of the inn felt like a rundown list instead of an experience through the FMC’s eyes. I also question some of SBD’s choices for the narrative:
Like, why did we focus so much on pancakes and not more scenes with the only three guests? These are fantastical creatures from other dimensions/realms that are coming to a whimsical inn in the middle of a Vermont forest. Of course I want to hear what they have to say, and see what they choose to do. But we didn’t get enough of them.
We could have had significant themes about the importance of family, taking care of our elderly, fixing damaged relationships, and putting aside egos. That would have been more intriguing than realm hopping.

NITPICKY: Stuff I didn’t like
1. The Moms: I cannot state how much I was annoyed by Calisa’s two moms. First, I get it. Authors want to ‘represent’ certain groups. But reading ‘Mom-Kate’ and ‘Mom-Elise’ as she referenced them was clunky as heck. She even called them this to their faces. Wouldn’t one be ‘mom’ (which is Kate because she’s Auntie Zee’s niece) and the other simply, ‘Elise?’ Are we going to sit here and pretend Calisa doesn’t have a dad (or at least a sperm donor)? Not to mention, when FMC finally calls her moms because Auntie Zee is missing, Mom-Kate starts making Star Wars jokes/references instead of taking it seriously. It also would have been helpful if she asked, “is there a cat around? Cause that’s Auntie Zee.” Mom-Kate would have absolutely known her aunt can transform into a cat.

2. Miscommunication: I found it odd that the moms know Auntie Zee is a witch, that the inn contains portals to other realms, and they didn’t share any of this with their daughter before shipping her off for the summer. They also sent her there without Auntie Zee’s permission! (again, still harping on how awful these moms are). Once FMC was there, Auntie Zee also kept her in the dark. Miscommunication, or a lack of communication, can definitely help a story along (because if all the facts are presented at once that’s a lengthy exposition and we have nothing to explore) but I hate when entire plots rely on this miscommunication or there is no story or intrigue. That’s when it gets annoying and also unrealistic. (I don’t buy that 2 moms would send their underage daughter out of state on her own to a place she’s not even welcome or expected).

3. Dialogue: Yeah, didn’t love it. I felt like a lot of the dialogue was quirky for the sake of being quirky. I know that Jack grew up living at The Faraway Inn but the kid still has a social life, still goes to school. He’d have some social cues, no? So, when he first finds FMC stuck in a hole in the porch, I would expect him to jump into gear and get her out of there. Not stand around talking about cheese. In other places, the dialogue was just straight up cringe (“I’ll be your Obi-Wan”) and personally, I don’t like when novels make IRL references like Star Wars, or “I’m just a boy standing in front of a girl asking her to love him.” It takes me out of the story.

4. Kissy Face: So, FMC thinks she may be able to open a portal. Her mom tells her she has to ‘unlock something within herself.’ ‘Have an epiphany.’ It’s purposely vague so Calisa is confused and doesn’t know what to do. Until, she looks at Jack and asks him to kiss her and that’s what does it. Again, it doesn’t require the FMC face any internal conflict, or make a sacrifice of any kind – she kisses the new love interest and boom, portal over here, portal over there. I don’t love overly feminist books, but even I was like, “wasn’t this supposed to be about her getting over a boy on her own volition, not by rebounding with the groundskeeper’s son?”

5. I’ll Retire When I’m Dead: So, Auntie Zee is described as being 80+. Her magic is failing, her time is running out, and instead of a little sympathy from Calisa, all our FMC does is question how/why Auntie Zee would let the inn fall into ruin? It came across as entirely selfish because she never once thinks about how Auntie Zee is feeling about all of this. All she brings up is actually how it affects Jack. He’s losing his home. Girl, this place is/was your great-aunt’s whole world. Why don’t you stop and reflect on how its current state is impacting her? Not only that, but Calisa just wanted the inn to keep going because ‘Well, I just got here.’ It was completely self-centered and actually made her a little less likable. She’s expecting her 82-year-old great-aunt to still be a mover and shaker when I think the old lady just wants to rest a bit.

6. WTF?: Um – is Jack’s dad in love with a statue? Er, moving on…

7. Questions Galore: When most of your novel is the FMC asking the same questions over and over again, or just mentally rehashing the same thoughts over and over again, you’ve got a problem. How many times were we reminded that “This is Jack’s home too,” or asked “Did Auntie Zee want the inn to close?” This story could have been a whopping 300 pages max if we deleted these inner monologues.

IN SUMMATION: This book was just okay.
Nothing more nothing less. 🥞🥞

Nothing about it really captivated me. I was never in a state of ‘I can’t wait to get back to ‘The Faraway Inn’ tonight.’ The characters didn’t feel like real people to me with realistic dialogue, or development. They didn’t really grow or change. It wasn’t exciting to read about making pancakes and which flavor of syrup they’d use today. And when we did get to what should have been thrilling, stepping through portals to unknown worlds, it fell flat because it didn’t impact the story. It was just a place for our FMC to be awed by before moving on. They weren’t exhilarating or developed because our leads didn’t stick around long enough to explore or get in trouble or anything remotely interesting like that.
​Cozy read? By definition, I suppose it checks the boxes. Maybe ‘cozy novels’ just aren’t for me since I crave action, excitement, character development, strong detailed writing, and a sense of accomplishment in the resolution. I want more than pancakes, dammit!

Calisa's looking for an escape this summer—she's recovering from a broken heart, and her great-aunt's inn, deep in Vermont without even a whisper of mobile data, seems like the place to be. Only: Aunt Zee doesn't want her there. And the inn has fallen into disrepair. And the closer Calisa looks, the more she understands that the inn is a little more...complicated...than Calisa first thought.

I read this largely on the strength of The Lake House, which gripped me by the throat for much of the book. The Faraway Inn is something else entirely—still a delight to speed through, but much more on the "charming" end of the scale than the "throat-gripping" end. I'm reminded of the phone game Matchington Mansion (which I did not reinstall when I had to get a new phone, because it is too much of a time suck), in which rooms gradually open up to the player...new place after new place to discover and restore. The inn isn't quite like that (we don't get enough details of, e.g., the library), but...at the same time, it kind of is. Every time a door opens, Calisa discovers something entirely new to her.

I was prepared for, I don't know, dark forces trying to bring the inn down, but the reality of the book is a lot calmer. There are problems, and Calisa ends up having to do quite a lot of problem-solving (and quite a lot of work), but not so much a Big Bad. I could have used a little more by way of details about what went wrong and how they're sure there's a long-term fix, but the general vibe is just very cozy in a way that turned out to be just what I was looking for in a book at the time.

Thanks to the author and publisher for providing a review copy through NetGalley.

Okay so I went into this book thinking it was going to be one of those cute and fun reads that I rate 3 stars and forget in like 5 seconds. While it was SO cute and fun it definitely wasn’t forgetful for me AT ALL. I’m usually the type of person who gets bored while reading a lot due to my very low attention span, so I was so SURPRISED when I didn’t get bored for even a second? if I had to describe to you my dream book before I read this, it would be exactly this. It seriously felt like a big warm hug and exactly what I needed. The second you open the book you immediately get transported into the story and oh my gosh all the cozy vibe are so there. It feels like ur a guest at the inn and experiencing everything side by side with the characters. All the characters were so likeable and the plot twists HIT HARD.

I screamed when we finally got the magical element to this. The portals? The magical mirror? Steve? The guests from different realms? Everything was perfection. my jaw was on the floor from so many parts of this. It was so nice to read a magical fantasy book that doesn’t have any world building or politics. Don’t get me wrong I love those things in books but I honestly just needed a break with something easy to read but also such a magical and fun journey and this was exactly that. Right after I finished I went and reread all my favourite scenes and that’s how you know I loved it. I genuinely miss all these characters and this story so much already I can’t wait to reread.

⋆✴︎˚｡⋆𝘾𝘼𝙇𝙄𝙎𝘼 🦎🌱🐈‍⬛

Easily one of my FAVOURITE fmcs. I feel like she was so brave and strong but also so sweet and cared so much about other people’s feelings as well as her own. I loved every second of her character development and I want to read more about her so bad! When she screamed when she found Steve in the bathroom for the first time I was like “wow that’s so me core” and then she opened someone’s room without asking for permission just because she wanted to know what they were saying i was like “so she’s literally me”. And then she continued to do things which I would totally do which made me like her even more as a fmc. Even tho she’s kind of like me I aspire to be like her because wow she’s so cool.

⋆✴︎˚｡⋆𝙅𝘼𝘾𝙆 🍰🪏🪴

Jack is exactly my type in every way,shape and form. Oh my gosh he’s so cute and adorable and so cinnamon roll coded I loved his SO MUCH. When I tell you cried when I found out that his dad had been gone for so long and he was going through all of this on his own, I mean I seriously started crying. his reunion with his father was so precious omg. He may come off as a really emotionally weak person from the outside but he’s truly SO STRONG and he was dealing with so much but still kept himself happy through all of it. If that’s not strength I don’t know what is. He also cares so much about the people he loves and his love for cake made me smile because oh my gosh he was just so cute. ⋆✴︎˚｡⋆ 𝙅𝘼𝘾𝙆 + 𝘾𝘼𝙇𝙄𝙎𝘼 🪄✨🚪

Literally my everything. When they kissed I screamed so loud I bet my neighbour’s could hear me. They not only had the sweetest relationship but also the sweetest friendship and I was rooting for them from the moment they met. This was a SLOW BURN and by that I mean that they first held hands at like 40% at-least. but that just made it so much better for me because I loved seeing there friendship with each other play out. When Calisa asked Jack to kiss her I was giggling so hard I had to look around to made sure nobody was seeing me act this way about words on paper. There I say one of my favourite fiction couples of this year?

This is so underrated and everyone needs to read this! I fear I must read everything this author write now.

The Faraway Inn
by Sarah Beth Durst
Cozy YA Fantasy
Booktrovert eARC (NetGalley)
Pub Date: Mar 31, 2026
Random House Children's Books/Delacorte Press
Ages: 14+

After sixteen-year-old Calisa catches her boyfriend cheating on her, she goes to rural Vermont for the summer to spend time at her great-aunt's B&B, only to find out that Auntie Zee had never agreed for her to stay there, and the inn was rundown instead of the magical place in her memories.

Only allowed to stay a few nights, Calisa makes it her mission to show her aunt that she can help fix up the inn. Making pancakes and befriending the groundskeeper's son, Calisa starts to make herself known to the few guests staying there, but she starts to notice strange things about them, Auntie Zee, and the inn itself, something that seems magical.


While the main characters are teenagers, sadly, the adults also act like kids, thus making this a very cozy fantasy that both YA and adults would like. It moves along at a good and steady pace, and there's no violence, and the romance is clean and mostly filler.

The lead-up to the mystery was a slow build, though I felt 'Steve' should've had some more drama, but overall it keeps the reader curious.

The only character I didn't care for was the groundskeeper's son. He came across as flat and a lot younger than Calisa, even though he was supposed to be older.

With the wonderful world-building, I could see this becoming a series, one I would be interested in reading.

3 Stars

Across the very ordinary, very green guest room was an open closet door. And what was inside was not ordinary.

This was the perfect definition of Cozy Fantasy. I absolutely adored every second of this book. From the main characters, Calisa, Jack, and Auntie Zee, to Steve the lizard dragon, the Wheeping Angel, the teapot, the Inn's guests, the magical ladder, and asshole mirror. It was light-hearted but deeply emotional down to its core.

4.75 stars

“You’re allowed to grow up at your own pace.”

From the afternoon tea, cleaning the rooms, planting seedlings, and saving the ocean, this exceeded my expectations. It was about growth and moving on, aging and beginning, life and living. It was filled with romance, whimsy, raspberry jam, chocolate cake, tea, peace, coziness, and comfort.

Allow yourself to feel what your heart wishes to feel. Do not deny your pain.

I loved Calisa and Jack as characters. I thought they both brought things to the story. And I felt so bad for Jack! Auntie Zee was great, what a grumpy, determined woman who didn’t want to ask for help.

Thank you so much to Random House and the author for this ARC!
